title: Anaesthesia for Patients with Complex Needs

references.label: Equality Act 2010
references.citation: Equality Act 2010 (UK). Places an anticipatory duty on service providers, including healthcare, to make reasonable adjustments so that disabled people are not placed at a substantial disadvantage.

references.label: MCA 2005
references.citation: Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales). Sets out the presumption of capacity, the requirement to support decision-making, the best-interests framework, and the conditions under which restraint is lawful (necessary to prevent harm and proportionate to its likelihood and seriousness).

references.label: NICE CG142 Autism
references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Autism spectrum disorder in adults: diagnosis and management. NICE clinical guideline CG142; 2012 (updated 2021). Includes adjustments to the physical and sensory environment and communication when delivering care.

references.label: NICE NG11 Challenging Behaviour
references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Challenging behaviour and learning disabilities: prevention and interventions for people with learning disabilities whose behaviour challenges. NICE guideline NG11; 2015. Emphasises identifying unmet physical and environmental needs before pharmacological interventions.

references.label: Vlassakova Autism 2016
references.citation: Vlassakova BG, Emmanouil DE. Perioperative considerations in children with autism spectrum disorder. Curr Opin Anaesthesiol. 2016;29(3):359-366. Reviews sensory and communication adaptation, premedication choice and reduction of restraint.

references.label: LeDeR 2023
references.citation: Learning from Lives and Deaths - People with a Learning Disability and Autistic People (LeDeR) annual report. King's College London / NHS England. Documents reduced life expectancy, avoidable deaths and recurring themes including diagnostic overshadowing and poor coordination of care.

references.label: RCoA GPAS 2023
references.citation: Royal College of Anaesthetists. Guidelines for the Provision of Anaesthesia Services (GPAS). Recommends identified pathways, staff training and service arrangements for patients with additional needs, including learning disability and autism.

references.label: NICE NG57 Prison Health
references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Physical health of people in prison. NICE guideline NG57; 2016. Sets out the principle of healthcare equivalent to that available to the wider population, continuity of care on transfer or release, and medicines management in custody.

references.label: NICE NG66 Criminal Justice
references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Mental health of adults in contact with the criminal justice system. NICE guideline NG66; 2017. Addresses the high prevalence of mental illness and substance misuse and the need for early assessment and liaison.

references.label: FFLM Restraint 2022
references.citation: Faculty of Forensic and Legal Medicine of the Royal College of Physicians. Guidance on the use of restraint and the healthcare of detainees, including removal of mechanical restraints for clinical procedures unless a documented security risk assessment requires otherwise.

cards.question: Can a family member or paid carer consent to anaesthesia for an adult with a learning disability?
cards.answer: No. No adult can consent on behalf of another in England and Wales unless they hold a valid Lasting Power of Attorney for health and welfare or are a court-appointed deputy. If the patient lacks capacity for the decision, treatment proceeds as a best-interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, consulting family and carers, and involving an IMCA where there is no one appropriate to consult.

cards.question: Is it ever lawful to hold an adult still for induction of anaesthesia?
cards.answer: Yes, but only where the patient lacks capacity for that decision, the holding is necessary to prevent harm to them, and the degree and duration are proportionate to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. It should be planned in advance with named roles, documented in the best-interests record, minimised by premedication and adjustments, and reviewed afterwards.

cards.question: What is a hospital passport and why does it matter to the anaesthetist?
cards.answer: It is a patient-held document summarising how someone with a learning disability or autism communicates, what distresses or calms them, how they show pain, their usual medication and their support needs. It converts a chaotic day-of-surgery encounter into a planned one and should be read before the patient arrives, not after.

cards.question: What should I do before reaching for sedation in a patient who cannot cooperate?
cards.answer: Work up the ladder: environmental and scheduling adjustments first, then preparation and desensitisation, distraction and control-giving, topical or local anaesthesia, regional techniques where suitable, and self-administered nitrous oxide/oxygen — with pharmacological premedication and inhalational induction reserved for when these are insufficient. Document which rung succeeded so it becomes the starting point next time.

cards.question: How do I consent a patient who communicates non-verbally?
cards.answer: Start the consent process early and in stages; provide easy-read, pictorial or video information; involve the people who know how the patient communicates; and use every support available (communication passport, AAC devices, interpreters, a trusted supporter) before concluding the patient cannot decide. If capacity for the decision is still lacking, hold a documented best-interests meeting with an IMCA if appropriate — a carer cannot simply sign instead.

cards.question: Should a prisoner's handcuffs be removed for surgery?
cards.answer: In almost all cases yes: metal restraints obstruct safe positioning, vascular access, diathermy, imaging and emergency airway management. Ask the escorting officers to remove them for induction, surgery and recovery. If a documented security risk assessment insists they remain, record the discussion and require an officer with the key to be immediately available in theatre.

cards.question: Do prisoners have the same confidentiality rights as other patients?
cards.answer: Yes. Custody officers may need operational information (timings, likely admission, whether the patient will be sedated) but not the diagnosis, drug history or infection status. Consultation should take place out of hearing whenever the security risk assessment allows.
